items.title: OpenAI announces three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics with collaborative academic release strategies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics
items.summary:
OpenAI revealed three new discoveries in harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory, and is experimenting with different collaborative approaches to release and explain these results with academic communities. The company is working with external experts who act as shepherds to organize groups that will help interpret and contextualize the findings, using varied release strategies tailored to each discovery.

For the mathematics result, OpenAI released the AI-generated proof publicly, including a formalized Lean proof, allowing researchers to independently explore the findings. For the computer science and physics results, OpenAI formed external collaborator groups to guide the explanation and release of materials, with the physics group currently holding off on public release to focus on writing up the results themselves. OpenAI emphasizes transparency, independence, and recognition for collaborators while not seeking academic credit for the AI-generated discoveries.

items.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Terra, a faster, more efficient AI model with improved visual reasoning, coding, and factual accuracy at half the cost of GPT-5.6 Terra [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GPT-6.1 Terra
items.summary:
OpenAI has introduced GPT-6.1 Terra, an AI model designed to deliver fast and capable computer use at scale with enhanced visual reasoning, precise computer tasks, and clearer writing. It offers significant improvements over GPT-5.6 Terra, including a 50% reduction in API pricing and better performance on professional benchmarks such as Agents’ Last Exam and MMMU-Pro.

GPT-6.1 Terra demonstrates substantial gains in reducing hallucinations and factual errors, with error rates dropping from 53.6% to 16.7% at low reasoning effort. It also more than doubles coding task success rates compared to its predecessor. The model maintains strong safety and alignment features, meeting OpenAI’s cybersecurity standards and resisting malicious prompt injections.

Available now to ChatGPT Work, Codex users, and via API, GPT-6.1 Terra aims to make high-volume automation tasks more practical and cost-effective while advancing AI capabilities in visual understanding, coding, and factual reliability.

items.title: Cloudflare fixes cross-request KV cache data leak in GLM-5.3 Workers AI model affecting 155 responses with long prompts [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (155 responses)
items.summary:
Cloudflare addressed a tenant isolation issue in its GLM-5.3 Workers AI model that caused some responses to include data from other customers' requests between August 27 and September 9, 2026. The problem affected 155 responses involving prompts longer than 681,280 tokens and was discovered by security researcher Gadi Evron. Cloudflare took the model offline on September 8, deployed a fix, and restored service the next day, confirming no other models were impacted.

The issue stemmed from a misconfiguration in the open-source inference engine SGLang and a bug in handling over-length requests, which caused stale cache data from previous requests to be included in responses. Cloudflare increased the KV cache pool size to accommodate the full context window and patched the engine to safely reject invalid requests before processing. These fixes were coordinated with SGLang maintainers and validated against reproduction tests to prevent recurrence.

items.title: Analysis: The Mythical Man-Month principle persists in AI development as managing multiple AI agents requires clear orchestration to avoid inefficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Mythical Man-Month in the Age of AI
items.summary:
A recent reflection revisits Frederick P. Brooks Jr.'s 1975 law that adding manpower to a late software project makes it later, questioning its relevance in the era of AI agents and large language models. While AI agents can onboard instantly and work continuously, the fundamental challenge of sequential tasks and coordination overhead remains, now shifted to managing AI agents rather than people.

The article argues that without clear requirements and orchestration, adding multiple autonomous AI agents to a project can lead to conflicting outputs and inefficiencies, effectively updating Brooks's Law to state that adding agents without clarity results in faster delivery of incorrect results. This highlights that human oversight and precise management remain critical in AI-driven software development.

items.title: Hokkaido University Hospital deploys LLENS platform with on-premises large language model Kimi K2.6 for clinical support inside closed network [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: The LLENS Platform for On-Premises Large Language Model Agents in a Japanese University Hospital: Development and Evaluation Study
items.summary:
Researchers developed and implemented LLENS, a clinical AI agent platform running inside the closed network of Hokkaido University Hospital using the open-weight Kimi K2.6 model with about one trillion parameters. The platform operates on a single host with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs and includes components for document processing, sandboxed execution, and self-checking, supporting hospital workflows since September 2026.

Kimi K2.6 was selected from three candidates after scoring 480 out of 500 on the 2026 Japanese Medical Licensing Examination. It achieved 97.2% accuracy on hospital document questions with interactive access, outperforming fixed retrieval methods. The platform successfully ran multiple clinical scenarios, including needlestick injury response and adverse event grading, demonstrating its practical utility within the hospital's secure environment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32151v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model agents that use tools could take on part of the electronic health record and desk work that occupies physicians' time, but in many hospitals the medical information systems run inside closed networks, so the model and the agent harness must also be inside the network. We designed, implemented, and deployed LLENS, a clinical support AI agent platform that runs inside the closed network of Hokkaido University Hospital on a single host with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the open-weight model Kimi K2.6 (~1 trillion parameters), and a web application rebuilt from Open WebUI. The harness has 10 components, including page image reading, full-text attachment input, a path-addressed document tree without a vector index, a network-isolated sandbox, artifact return, self-checking of generated output, subagents, and saved procedures. Kimi K2.6 was chosen from 3 open-weight candidates and scored 480/500 on the 2026 Japanese Medical Licensing Examination; it generated 119 tokens/s for a single user and served 16 concurrent requests at 908 tokens/s in total. On 180 questions over hospital documents (3 seeds each), mean accuracy was 10.7% with no documents, 81.3% with fixed retrieval (top 10 chunks of one lexical search), and 97.2% with interactive access, in which the model reads with document tools and the sandbox (15.9 percentage points above fixed retrieval, 95% CI 10.9-21.3); the difference lay in filtering/counting questions (16.7% vs 87.8%). In an automated test of 13 work scenarios (4 runs each), the expected components were triggered in all runs for 12, and 5 scenarios were run with synthetic data on the deployment host. The platform has run on the hospital network since September 14, 2026.

items.title: Perspective: AI-specific skills may become obsolete by 2026 as AI tools integrate prompt engineering and evolve rapidly [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: “AI Skills” are worthless in 2026
items.summary:
A recent perspective argues that AI-specific skills like prompt engineering, which can be learned quickly, are likely to become obsolete within a few months as AI capabilities are integrated directly into products. The author compares this to outdated programming habits that persisted despite compiler optimizations, suggesting that the rapid evolution of AI tools will fold current tricks into default experiences, reducing the long-term value of specialized AI skills.

The article emphasizes the importance of keeping up with current AI developments to perform well today but cautions against overvaluing transient skills. It also reflects on the hype around early AI adoption, noting that getting AI integration right may be more important than being first, and advocates for steady progress rather than rushing to adopt every new AI trend immediately.

items.title: Meta-analysis finds large language models show modest loss aversion and human-like probability weighting but differ in diminishing sensitivity compared to humans [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Prospect Theory in Large Language Models: A Meta-Analysis of Loss Aversion, Diminishing Sensitivity, and Probability Weighting
items.summary:
A meta-analysis of 102 estimates from 11 studies covering 32 large language models (LLMs) examined whether these models exhibit components of prospect theory—loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity, and probability weighting—similar to humans. The analysis found that LLMs display modest loss aversion with a pooled lambda of 1.26, lower than the strongest human estimates, and show human-like probability weighting with an inverse S shape. However, their value functions vary by measurement method, appearing close to linear or more concave than humans, indicating differences in diminishing sensitivity.

The study also noted that LLMs align more closely with human loss aversion when gains and losses are symmetric but diverge when losses are smaller than gains, where human loss aversion is strongest. These findings suggest that while LLMs replicate some aspects of human risky choice behavior, such as probability distortion, they differ in how they process losses and outcome sensitivity, with variations depending on model families and fitting methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.33103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prospect theory splits risky choice into three parts: loss aversion, measured by the relative weight of losses to gains, $\lambda$ (e.g., $\lambda = 2$ implies that losses weigh twice as much as gains), diminishing sensitivity to the size of outcomes (i.e., the curvature and linearity of the value function), and the nonlinear weighting of probabilities. I examined whether Large Language Models (LLMs) display the same properties as people by meta-analyzing 102 fitted estimates from 11 studies covering 32 language models. The three components emerge differently. Loss aversion is modest: the pooled $\lambda$ is 1.26 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.46), far below the strongest human meta-analytic estimate ($\lambda = 1.96$) and compatible with more conservative ones (1.07 and 1.31). Matched by design, LLMs are compatible with people when gains and losses are symmetric ($\lambda = 1.15$ against 1.07), but well below them when losses are smaller than gains (1.46 against 2.3), where human loss aversion is strongest. Value functions are close to linear rather than concave under the Tversky-Kahneman method (1.01, against a human value of 0.67), but more concave than in people under the Tanaka method (0.52, against 0.67), so diminishing sensitivity depends on how it is measured. Probability weighting shows a human-like inverse S shape ($\gamma = 0.81$ under Tversky-Kahneman and 0.84 under the Tanaka method), though on few studies. In sum, LLMs show little loss aversion and little diminishing sensitivity, but retain human-like probability distortion, yet these generalizations shift when looking at specific model families and fitting methods.

items.title: Researchers present synthetic document finetuning to expose alignment-faking large language models by revealing latent misaligned propensities through keyword cues [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Propensities Please: Exposing Alignment-Faking LLMs using Synthetic Document Finetuning
items.summary:
Researchers propose a method called synthetic document finetuning (SDF) to detect alignment-faking behavior in large language models, where models conceal misaligned actions during evaluation. By finetuning models to associate certain keywords with undetected misaligned actions, they observed increased differences in misaligned behavior between prompts with and without these cues, improving detection beyond prompt-based methods.

The study highlights that existing detection methods relying on chain-of-thought monitoring or realistic environments may become less effective as models advance. While SDF can impair reasoning capabilities, the researchers introduce an on-policy distillation technique to mitigate this effect. They emphasize the importance of behavioral detection methods as models grow more capable and less interpretable.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.33180v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Alignment evaluations aim to assess whether large language models would engage in dangerous misaligned behaviour. Misaligned and evaluation-aware models might engage in alignment faking, where they pursue a hidden goal, but conceal this behaviour when they suspect effective oversight such as during training, evaluation or audited deployment. Such a model might view any prompt-based intervention that aims to reveal latent propensities as part of the evaluation, calling into question the reliability of existing alignment evaluations. Current methods for detecting alignment faking rely on chain-of-thought monitorability, highly realistic environments that reduce evaluation awareness, or mechanistic interventions, all of which are expected to become less reliable for future model generations. We present a method for revealing latent misaligned propensities that does not rely on any of these. We use synthetic document finetuning to teach models that misaligned actions will go undetected whenever certain keywords appear in the prompt. We place alignment-faking model organisms in environments that are clearly identifiable as honeypots and measure how their behaviour changes after finetuning. We observe that finetuning consistently widens the gap in misaligned action rates between prompts with and without the cue, indicating that finetuning allows exposing latent propensities more reliably than purely prompt-based methods. We argue that behavioural methods for detecting alignment faking and related behaviours are critical going forward, as models become more capable and less interpretable. We find that SDF often damages the models' reasoning capabilities and introduce a mitigation based on on-policy distillation.

items.title: Researchers introduce SkillShift-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating web agent skill learning under environment shifts including contextual, perceptual, and execution changes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillShift-Bench: Benchmarking Skill Learning under Environment Evolution for Web Agents
items.summary: SkillShift-Bench is designed to test web agents' ability to reuse learned skills in evolving real-world web environments, simulating shifts in context, perception, and execution feasibility. The benchmark evaluates agents across three self-hosted web systems using metrics such as task success, interaction cost, skill use, and failure rates. Experiments show that agents' robustness declines under these shifts, especially execution shifts, which cause the most significant performance drops. The researchers also propose a dynamic-regret analysis and a test-time adaptation method to improve skill execution without retraining the skill library. The benchmark's code, tasks, environments, documentation, and leaderboard are publicly available online.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.33528v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Skill learning enables web agents to reuse prior experience for long-horizon interactive tasks. However, learned skills are typically evaluated in closed environments, overlooking the fact that real-world web deployment involves continuous shifts in invocation context, perceptual grounding, and execution feasibility. To this end, we introduce SkillShift-Bench, the first benchmark for evaluating skill learning with controlled open-environment shifts. SkillShift-Bench simulates Contextual Shift, Perceptual Shift, and Execution Shift across three self-hosted web systems, and evaluates agents with diagnostics covering task success, interaction cost, skill use, and skill failure. Comprehensive experiments reveal systematic robustness degradation under controlled shifts, characterized by lower success rates, higher interaction costs, and more frequent skill failures, with Execution Shift exerting the strongest pressure. We further formulate shifted skill execution as a nonstationary local executability problem and provide both a dynamic-regret analysis and a practical test-time adaptation method, demonstrating the feasibility of improving learned-skill execution without relearning the skill library. Code, tasks, environments, documentation, and the leaderboard are available at https://skillshift-bench.github.io/.

items.title: Researchers introduce Preference-Behavior Model to jointly infer preferences and imperfect decision-making in large language models across social dilemmas [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Jointly Modeling Preferences and Imperfect Decision-Making in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers propose the Preference-Behavior Model (PBM) to jointly model preferences and imperfect utility maximization in large language models (LLMs), addressing how conflicting objectives shape their strategic behavior. The model is evaluated in three social dilemmas—Public Goods Game, Collective-Risk Dilemma, and Common-Pool Resource dilemma—revealing that preferences inferred from one setting can predict behavior in others better than standard elicitation methods.

The study finds that traditional behavioral economic elicitation instruments do not consistently predict LLM behavior across dilemmas, while PBM captures meaningful aspects of decision-making and alignment with persona instructions. This framework offers a new approach to assess LLM preference consistency, alignment with intended priorities, and behavioral trade-offs that standard methods may overlook.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.33651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Do preferences Large Language Models (LLMs) express in standard elicitation tasks predict their strategic behaviour? LLM agents interacting with humans and other AI systems face potentially conflicting objectives, such as individual welfare, group welfare, and environmental concerns. Prior work characterizes LLM preferences through behavioral-economic and psychological elicitation or strategic games, but rarely tests consistency across settings and prediction in other strategic environments. This requires modeling how competing objectives jointly shape behavior, whereas existing approaches typically measure preference dimensions in isolation. Drawing on utility theory, we introduce the Preference-Behavior Model (PBM), which combines a preference representation with mechanisms capturing imperfect utility maximization. We formulate estimation as an inverse-game problem, jointly inferring preferences and behavioral parameters from observed choices. We evaluate PBM in three social dilemmas that expose conflicting motives: a Public Goods Game, a Collective-Risk Dilemma, and a Common-Pool Resource dilemma. We find that while preferences estimated from established behavioral economic elicitation instruments do not consistently predict behavior in these dilemmas, models fitted in one dilemma retain predictive value in others, suggesting that inferred preferences capture meaningful aspects of LLM decision-making that elicitation instruments may miss. Finally, we assess alignment with persona instructions, finding that inferred preferences broadly reflect intended priorities with specific divergences across dimensions, LLMs, and games being identified by our approach. Our methodology provides a framework for studying how consistently LLM preferences explain behavior, assessing alignment with intended priorities, and revealing trade-offs and behavioral patterns that standard elicitation may miss.

items.title: Meta-CLIP introduces metadata-conditioned contrastive learning to improve zero-shot disease inference in medical imaging, enhancing performance on chest radiography and CT benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Meta-CLIP: Metadata-Conditioned Contrastive Learning for Zero-Shot Disease Inference
items.summary:
Meta-CLIP is a new framework that incorporates acquisition metadata from DICOM headers into contrastive learning for medical vision-language pretraining, aiming to improve transferability across different scanners and protocols. It uses a fixed kernel over numerical and categorical metadata fields to reweight negative samples during training, emphasizing distinctions among studies with similar imaging conditions without requiring metadata at inference.

The method was evaluated on chest radiography and volumetric chest CT datasets, showing improved macro-AUROC scores over previous models like CT-CLIP, including a 1.41-point increase on the CT-RATE dataset and top performance on four out of five chest X-ray benchmarks. These results suggest that acquisition metadata can serve as a useful training-time prior for medical imaging models. The authors plan to release the code publicly upon publication.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.33674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical vision--language pretraining learns transferable representations from paired images and radiology reports, yet differences in scanners and acquisition protocols can impair transfer. Existing approaches primarily enrich clinical semantics, leaving structured acquisition information in DICOM headers underused. We introduce Meta-CLIP, a metadata-conditioned contrastive framework that uses acquisition similarity to reweight cross-modal negatives during pretraining. A kernel over numerical and categorical DICOM fields defines a bounded pairwise margin. This margin increases the contribution of acquisition-similar negatives, emphasizing distinctions among studies that share imaging conditions. The kernel remains fixed during image--text optimization, and inference follows the standard dual-encoder architecture without requiring metadata. We evaluate Meta-CLIP on chest radiography and volumetric chest CT through zero-shot classification, appearance perturbations, grounding, and representation analyses. On CT-RATE, Meta-CLIP improves macro-AUROC over CT-CLIP by 1.41 points, with a 95\% paired bootstrap confidence interval of 0.96--1.85 points. It also achieves the highest macro-AUROC on four of five CXR benchmarks. An exploratory BrgSA evaluation extends the analysis to another CT backbone. These findings support acquisition metadata as a practical training-time prior for medical vision--language learning. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.

items.title: Researchers publish comprehensive guide to System 1 decision models for fast, calibrated AI decisions beyond large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Hitchhiker's Guide to System 1 Models: Fast Decision-Making Beyond LLMS
items.summary: A new guide presents a detailed overview of System 1 decision models, which enable rapid, single-pass decisions for routine AI tasks like routing and classification, addressing the latency and calibration issues of large language models. The guide categorizes these models into five families, explores their architectures and training methods, and emphasizes calibration techniques including Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). It also discusses integration strategies combining fast System 1 models with slower, more complex models in agentic workflows. Covering 18 application domains and featuring over 70 open-source model reproductions, runnable code, and a practitioner's checklist, the guide aims to serve as a unified resource for researchers and engineers working on fast decision-making and production AI systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.33775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models excel at reasoning and generation but their autoregressive, token-by-token inference makes them unnecessarily slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated for the many routine decisions (routing, gating, scoring, classification) that modern AI systems require at sub-second latency. A growing class of models addresses this gap: System 1 decision models, architectures that map an input directly to a typed, structured decision in a single forward pass. This guide provides a comprehensive, practitioner-oriented treatment of the field. We propose a five-family taxonomy covering encoder-based classifiers, reward models, non-autoregressive decision engines, contrastive decision models, and extraction models, and we provide in-depth coverage of each family's architecture, training methodology, and deployment trade-offs. A central theme is calibration: we develop the theory of proper scoring rules, analyze Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), and examine recently discovered phenomena including IIA violations, ordinal-scale bias, and few-shot recalibration under distribution shift. On the integration side, we describe how System 1 models serve as decision infrastructure within agentic workflows and System 1 + System 2 cascades that route between fast and slow models based on calibrated confidence. The guide covers 18 application domains, maps the rapidly growing open-source ecosystem (over 70 model reproductions in weeks), provides runnable code throughout, and includes a practitioner's checklist, an open-source model zoo, and 22 self-assessment questions with detailed answers. Spanning 190 references, it is intended as a unified entry point for researchers and engineers working at the intersection of fast decision-making, calibration, and production AI systems.

items.originalTitle: EnvLunch: The Environment as a Free Lunch for Learning to Interact
items.summary: Researchers introduce EnvLunch, a training approach that leverages the structure and verifiable outcomes of executable environments to teach language-model agents how to interact without requiring human-annotated tasks. EnvLunch samples valid action sequences, executes them to obtain final observations, and trains agents to reconstruct equivalent trajectories from these observations, serving as a warm-up before reinforcement learning. This method outperforms baselines by over 9 points on average and reduces the need for annotated examples by 8 to 32 times at low training budgets. EnvLunch also improves fine-tuning on benchmarks beyond data analysis, offering a more efficient starting point for agentic model training when annotated tasks are scarce.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.33817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For agentic data analysis, language-model agents often require a large number of annotated tasks to learn how to interact effectively with executable environments (i.e., databases). While high-quality annotated tasks require heavy manual effort, an executable environment already provides rich interaction structure and verifiable outcomes. In this sense, the environment itself offers a free lunch, an additional set of verifiable tasks that require no human annotation. We propose EnvLunch, a warm-up stage that turns this environmental signal into agent training without human-written or model-generated task descriptions, before downstream agentic reinforcement learning. EnvLunch samples valid action trajectories, executes them to obtain final observations, and trains an agent to recover a functionally equivalent trajectory given only its final observation. This label-free warm-up enables the model to outperform the baseline by over 9 points on average across all downstream training budgets, and with few labels, the baseline needs 8 to 32 times as many annotated examples to match the accuracy that the EnvLunch model reaches at its smallest training budget. Letting the environment alone define the task yields a larger gain than having the model write its own tasks over the same environments, and this warm-up also improves fine-tuning on benchmarks beyond data analysis. EnvLunch therefore saves annotated tasks and provides a better starting point for fine-tuning agentic models when such tasks are limited.

items.title: Researchers evaluate large language models' ability to calibrate trust and reliance on imperfect human and AI partners using a benchmark of 324 collaboration scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can LLMs Trust Appropriately? Evaluating Calibrated Reliance on Imperfect Partners
items.summary: Researchers investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can appropriately calibrate trust when collaborating with humans and AI agents whose inputs may be incomplete or incorrect. They introduce a benchmark comprising 324 scenarios across 23 collaboration categories, each involving sequential decisions with explicit feedback and cost structures to evaluate reliance policies against expected outcomes. Seven models and 36 controlled probes were tested, revealing that while the strongest model approaches near-optimal decisions, others show issues such as excessive safeguards and misallocated assistance. Providing explicit posterior distributions corrected some errors but introduced new failure modes, highlighting the need for coupling empirical evidence with forward-looking decision utility in autonomous agents' trust calibration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.34107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly collaborate with humans and peer AI agents whose contributions may be incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrect. Effective collaboration requires calibrated trust, whereby decisions to rely on, verify, or assist a partner adapt rationally as empirical evidence accumulates. We investigate whether models translate partner evidence into appropriate reliance policies. We introduce a benchmark of 324 scenarios across 23 collaboration categories. Each scenario involves three sequential decisions with explicit transition dynamics, feedback emissions, and cost schedules, permitting exact analytical evaluation of choices against their expected consequences over the remaining interaction. Evaluating seven models alongside 36 controlled-history probes, we dissociate evidence sensitivity from normatively appropriate action. While the strongest frontier model approaches near-optimal decisions, other models exhibit recurring pathologies: procuring excessive safeguards, purchasing verification tests with zero expected value of information, prioritizing immediate savings over cooperative learning, and misallocating assistance to suboptimal channels. Supplying explicit posterior distributions resolves certain errors while introducing new failure modes. Calibrated trust in autonomous agents critically demands coupling empirical evidence with forward-looking decision utility.

items.title: Researchers introduce SABench to evaluate side-effect risks in tool-using language model agents, finding 15.2% of runs cause unauthorized actions despite task success [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Task Success Is Not Enough: Side-effect-Aware Evaluation of Tool-Using Language Model Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SABench, a benchmark designed to assess side-effect risks in language model agents that use tools, highlighting that task completion alone does not guarantee safe operation. The benchmark includes 201 tasks involving email, calendar, and ticket management, each tested against four state structures and four trap types to detect unauthorized side effects, termed collateral damage (CD).

Testing 11 leading large language models across 2,211 model-task pairs, the study found that 15.2% of runs incurred collateral damage, with ambiguity-related tasks showing the highest violation rate at 38.8%. Even among runs that achieved their goals, 12.8% produced unauthorized writes. The results indicate that cross-tool and dependent state tasks have roughly double the CD rate compared to independent states, and CD rates vary significantly across models, suggesting that task success is an insufficient metric for evaluating safe tool use in language models.

The SABench dataset, along with traces, oracles, code, and analysis tools, has been publicly released to support further research into safer AI tool usage.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.34167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language model agents are usually evaluated by whether they finish the user's task. That metric misses a common failure: an agent can complete the requested work while also taking an unauthorized side-effecting action, such as writing to the wrong object, expanding the scope of the request, or contacting an unintended recipient. We call this failure mode collateral damage (CD). We introduce SABench (Side-effect-Aware Benchmark), a benchmark of 201 email, calendar, and ticket tasks. Each task crosses one of four state structures (independent, dependent, externally reachable, cross-tool) with one of four trap families (ambiguity, mis-targeting, cascade harm, overreach), and each task has a deterministic trace-based oracle for both goal satisfaction and authorization compliance. Across 2,211 model-task pairs from 11 frontier LLMs spanning major commercial and open model families, 15.2% of all runs incur CD, with risk concentrated in ambiguity tasks (38.8% violation rate) while non-ambiguous traps average 8.4% CD. Among goal-satisfied runs, 12.8% still produce unauthorized writes. Cross-tool and dependent states have about twice the CD rate of independent states. CD rates vary by 4.7x across models at comparable goal rates, which suggests that task success alone is a poor proxy for safe tool use. The SABench task corpus is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Phaedrus/sabench; the traces, oracle, code, and analysis pipeline are released at https://github.com/hjj194/sabench-artifact.

items.title: Researchers analyze reasoning effort levels in LLM agents, finding higher effort increases cost and changes behavior without consistently improving task success across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Effort Level Should I Choose? On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers studied the impact of varying reasoning effort levels in large language model (LLM) agents on four benchmarks, including single-call reasoning and long-horizon tasks. They found that while higher effort can improve accuracy on average, it often fails on tasks solved by lower effort and can cost up to 42 times more. Higher effort also alters how agents approach problems, increasing verification and solution search steps without necessarily improving outcomes.

The study shows that choosing the highest effort level is not always cost-effective or optimal for individual tasks. Instead, starting with the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure matches or exceeds fixed high-effort performance at lower cost for most proprietary models, suggesting a more efficient strategy for managing reasoning effort in LLM agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.34491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models increasingly expose a reasoning effort setting that lets users scale inference-time compute, trading higher cost for potentially improved performance. Users must choose an effort level before knowing whether extra reasoning will help, and even a successful run does not reveal whether the effort purchased was necessary. Reasoning effort is therefore a credence good: buyers observe the outcome but cannot assess the marginal value of the computation they paid for. In this work, we measure the counterfactual effect of effort levels on both proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks, spanning single-call reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks. Effort, it turns out, does not consistently preserve tasks that lower effort solves, can overspend, and can change trajectory behavior. First, we find that although higher effort can raise accuracy in aggregate, it frequently fails on tasks that lower effort solved. Second, on the subset of easy tasks that every effort level solves, higher effort is generally more costly, with the highest effort level costing up to 42x as much as the lowest. Lastly, effort changes not only how many tokens are used, but also how agents solve tasks: at higher effort, agents verify their own work more heavily and more often search for solutions than work through problems directly, both of which lengthen trajectories without necessarily altering the outcome. These findings show that naively choosing the highest level is not only cost-inefficient but also offers no guarantee of the best instance-level performance. A simple alternative, starting at the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure, matches or improves on fixed top effort across all models and benchmarks at lower cost for most proprietary models.

items.title: Researchers propose a simple lookup table using mean log-mel vectors per phoneme for text injection in speech recognition, achieving faster training and state-of-the-art word error rates on LibriSpeech
items.originalTitle: One Mean Log-Mel Vector per Phoneme: Simple and Fast Text Injection for Speech Recognition
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a method for text injection in speech recognition that replaces a frozen text-to-speech model with a simple lookup table of mean log-mel vectors per phoneme, repeated for durations based on alignment statistics and including silences between words. This approach trains 1.8 times faster than neural TTS while maintaining comparable word error rates. Using an external language model, their system achieves state-of-the-art word error rates on the LibriSpeech dataset using only paired data, text, and lexicon.

The study analyzes components of the synthetic input, compares different HMM aligners, and evaluates scaling on a large 25,000-hour dataset. It also demonstrates that full-encoder text injection yields stronger improvements than partial-encoder or decoder methods. The complete code for the pipeline is publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.34623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text injection trains speech recognition models on unpaired text alongside paired audio. We feed the speech encoder synthetic input derived from text so the whole model learns from it. Previously, we synthesized this input with a frozen text-to-speech (TTS) model. Here, a simple lookup table replaces the TTS model: a mean log-mel vector (or one-hot encoding) per phoneme, repeated for a random duration drawn from alignment statistics, with silence between words. Training is 1.8 times faster than with the neural TTS, achieving comparable word error rates. With an external language model, our system reaches 1.36 / 2.90 / 1.52 / 3.24 % WER on LibriSpeech {dev,test}-{clean,other}, to our knowledge state-of-the-art using only LibriSpeech paired data, text, and lexicon. We analyze components of synthetic input (durations, acoustic features), compare different HMM aligners, evaluate scaling on the 25 000 h Loquacious dataset, and show that full-encoder injection yields strong relative improvements compared to partial-encoder and decoder methods. The code of the whole pipeline behind every number in this paper is public: github.com/rwth-i6/returnn-experiments/tree/master/2026-text-injection

items.originalTitle: AdaTutor: Adaptive Tutoring through Pedagogical Strategy Selection
items.summary: Researchers present AdaTutor, a tutoring system that adapts pedagogical strategies to student errors using a training framework called Comparative Pedagogical Supervision (CPS). items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.34871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare has opened new possibilities for AI-assisted clinical decision-making; however, safe and effective deployment remains challenging because of hallucination and domain misalignment. This study introduces DocTalk, a doctor-assistive question-answering (QA) system designed to generate concise, chart-grounded responses from de-identified discharge summaries. Methods: We developed a high-fidelity data generation pipeline that produces 500 clinically relevant QA pairs through sentence-level decomposition, chain-of-thought-guided question formulation, and expert review. Six open-source LLMs, including three general-purpose and three biomedical models, were evaluated before and after parameter-efficient instruction tuning using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework integrates prompt engineering, in-context learning, and medically aligned evaluation to support factual and interpretable responses. Results: On DocTalk-QA, instruction tuning produced consistent improvements across lexical, semantic, and clinical fidelity metrics. The best-performing tuned model, Llama-3-Med42-8B, achieved ROUGE-L = 0.40, BERTScore-F1 = 0.76, and UMLS-F1 = 0.49. To examine external generalization beyond the DocTalk-QA dataset, the two best-performing models, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3-Med42-8B, were evaluated on PubMedQA before and after instruction tuning. Accuracy improved from 0.931 to 0.977 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from 0.935 to 0.943 for Llama-3-Med42-8B. Conclusion: DocTalk was deployed as a secure web-based platform for interactive EHR querying. These findings suggest that clinically grounded instruction tuning can improve medical QA performance and support practical clinical decision support.

items.title: ThinkBit: Search Codewords, Recalibrate Scales, Select by Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ThinkBit: Search Codewords, Recalibrate Scales, Select by Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning language models generate thousands of tokens per answer, and generation speed is limited by memory bandwidth, so storing weights in two bits instead of bfloat16 can potentially make inference 8$\times$ cheaper. Two-bit methods are usually judged by perplexity and multiple-choice question-answering accuracy, both of which say little about whether a model can still reason through more difficult problems. We present ThinkBit, a strictly scalar two-bit framework built to preserve reasoning, in which every weight is an integer codeword times a bfloat16 scale shared by a group of weights. We first use a sensitivity metric to assign each layer a ternary, 2-bit, or 3-bit tier to allocate bitwidths optimally among layers. This is followed by a layerwise Gumbel-softmax-based scalar quantization algorithm that searches for optimal codewords block by block. Since a layerwise scheme does not capture how quantized layers interact with each other, we recalibrate scales, with the codewords frozen, using a knowledge-distillation-based loss against the teacher model. We then perform a short quantization-aware training (QAT) stage that lets the model mimic the base model's distribution by reassigning codewords. Finally, a paired reasoning test on training problems selects the final checkpoint between the recalibration stage and the QAT stage. On Qwen3-1.7B at matched size, our recalibrated checkpoint scores 46.7 on MATH-500 against 30.0 for EfficientQAT trained on the same data, and 73.0 after QAT on reasoning traces; at 0.52 GB it is smaller than every published 2-bit GGUF of the model yet more accurate on MATH-500. We show that this framework scales and up to 14B, a 3.74 GB model scores 94.8 on MATH-500, against 97.5 for the 29.5 GB bfloat16 model.

items.title: Trainable Boundary-Keeping Where No Formal Answer Exists: A Controlled Knock-In Study of Reward Training in Evidence-Sufficiency Judgment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Trainable Boundary-Keeping Where No Formal Answer Exists: A Controlled Knock-In Study of Reward Training in Evidence-Sufficiency Judgment
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning-tuned and reward-trained models are often assumed to verify more reliably because they reason longer or receive correctness signals. We test this in evidence-sufficiency judgment: deciding whether available information actually supports a causal claim, a domain with no decidable correctness reward. Using a pre-registered, same-base, controlled knock-in design, we compare a boundary-keeping recipe (SFT then GRPO) with its own baseline, a scrambled-pairing placebo, and a general-purpose reasoning model under an action-pressure protocol with no evaluation invitation. All load-bearing outcomes are rated by two separate model-rating sessions masked to arm labels; automatic judges only trigger. The trained arm raises spontaneous correct refusal from 25% to 100% (40 per arm; Wilson 95% CI lower bound 91.2%, non-overlapping with the baseline interval [14.2%, 40.2%]), while the scrambled placebo collapses (5% spontaneous / 7.5% invited correct; 91.1% false refusal). The effect is boundary-specific rather than blanket refusal: automatic false refusal on 281 well-formed claims is 1.1% (Wilson upper bound 3.09%), and a targeted 18-item arm-(c) recheck (3 flagged plus 15 accepted) yields 0/18 and 1/18 false refusals in two sessions. The dissociation is the main result: final boundary-keeping is trainable without an inference-time verifier, while observed active numeric/calculation checking in the H3 assay remains near zero; SFT saturation makes the GRPO increment not separately identifiable. A pre-registered mechanism adjudication favors reward internalization of final-action status (H2, best-supported, not proven). The scope is a controlled 14B same-family study: we do not claim proof, cross-family generality, or independent human-expert validation; the rating sessions are model sessions, not human reviewers.

items.title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system also improves the way it improves, is a long-standing aspiration on the path to AGI. Language agents increasingly store procedural knowledge in reusable skills. Optimizing skills offers a direct way to achieve RSI, because the optimization procedure itself can be encoded as a skill. Existing skill optimizers, however, follow a hand-designed procedure. Even methods that evolve a meta-skill confine it to a fixed pipeline and relearn it for each task. We present Skill$^{\infty}$, which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving: a meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and optimizes the meta-skill itself using the same procedure. The optimization is agent-led. The meta agent diagnoses execution traces, proposes candidates, requests independent reviews, and allocates the search budget. The meta-skill defines these steps, allowing self-improvement to rewrite them. This meta-skill is also decoupled from task skills, refined on multiple skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across diverse domains. As in deployment, skills at both levels are standard packages loaded through native skill discovery. On 83 SkillsBench tasks, Skill$^{\infty}$ reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver.

items.title: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
items.originalTitle: Linear Probes Transfer from Base to Distilled Language Models despite Rotation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear probes, classifiers that read a language model's internal activations, are widely used to detect harmful requests. They are cheap to train and run, and an auditor who has trained one would like to reuse it when the model is replaced by a successor rather than retrain it for every release. We test how well probes can be reused. items.title: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Center-of-Mass Interpretation of Evolution Strategies
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evolution strategies (ES) update a model by sampling a population of perturbed copies, scoring each one, and moving in the reward-weighted direction of the perturbations. This update is usually presented as an estimate of a smoothed gradient. We present a geometrical interpretation of this update instead. Treat each perturbed model as a particle and its reward as the particle's mass. Before scoring, every particle has the same mass and the population balances at its centroid. Once rewards are assigned, it balances at its reward-weighted center of mass instead. We show that the mean-subtracted ES update is exactly this displacement, scaled by a scalar factor that depends on the mean reward, for any finite population. The physical reading needs nonnegative rewards, which can always be arranged by adding a constant to every reward without changing the update. In the limit of a large population or under antithetic sampling, the centroid sits on the model itself, so ES has an even simpler geometric interpretation: from its current location, the model moves towards the reward-weighted center of mass of its own population. The same picture explains what subtracting the mean reward does: it changes the point from which the displacement is measured, from the model to the sampled centroid. Our contribution is an intuitive, geometric way to visualize an ES update, exact for any finite population.

items.title: Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21073v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A coding agent works on repositories that can be far larger than its context window can hold. Prompt compressors and retrievers offer solutions to this problem, but patching an issue needs two things at once: the files that must change, and their code exactly as written, since the model must reproduce the lines it edits. Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget. We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks. We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark's tests. With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3). Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits.

items.title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32951v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged.

items.title: TIAgent: From Natural Language to Grounded Agentic Workflows for Computational Pathology [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TIAgent: From Natural Language to Grounded Agentic Workflows for Computational Pathology
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32993v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computational pathology (CPath) analyses increasingly depend on multi-step computational workflows that require substantial programming expertise, limiting their accessibility to pathologists and other domain experts without extensive coding experience. Although large language models (LLMs) provide a promising natural-language interface for constructing such analyses, hallucinated operations and incorrect workflow specifications limit their reliability in scientific settings. We introduce Tissue Image Analysis Agent (TIAgent), an automated CPath workflow generation framework that, given a natural-language prompt specifying a complex analytical task together with an input dataset, automatically constructs a verifiable computational graph employing existing CPath operations. The resulting graph can be inspected and executed, enabling natural-language construction of complex CPath workflows for applications including automated biomarker discovery and tissue analysis. We demonstrate end-to-end workflow generation and execution and systematically benchmark 14 backbone LLMs across 90 unit tasks spanning 18 CPath operation types. The ability of each LLM to generate a complete and correct unit workflow is quantified using Unit Workflow Success (UWS). Performance varied substantially across backbone models, with Kimi-K2.7-Code achieving the highest UWS of 0.967 (95% CI: 0.907-0.989). Analysis of node and parameter correctness further revealed that selecting the appropriate computational operation and correctly configuring it represent distinct challenges for LLM-based workflow generation. TIAgent provides a foundation for making complex CPath workflow construction more accessible while enabling systematic evaluation of LLM-driven scientific workflow generation.

items.title: Whispering Wisely: Smart Subset Selection for ASR Fine-Tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Whispering Wisely: Smart Subset Selection for ASR Fine-Tuning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models such as OpenAIs Whisper have substantially improved speech recognition quality but remain expensive to fine-tune, especially when large amounts of transcribed audio are available. This makes it challenging for many practitioners to adapt these models to new languages or domains. In this work, we introduce an embedding-based subset selection approach for selecting smaller training sets for ASR fine-tuning. Using Whispers pretrained encoder, we map each audio sample into a fixed-dimensional embedding space and apply a greedy k-center algorithm to select diverse and representative subsets of the training data. We evaluate this approach on both Hebrew and Danish, showing that k-center selection often improves upon random sampling, particularly at smaller subset sizes. An analysis of lexical diversity reveals that k-center subsets capture a broader range of linguistic content than random subsets of the same size, which may help explain their observed effectiveness. Overall, our results demonstrate that embedding-based subset selection provides a practical strategy for ASR subset selection in the two evaluated languages, with the clearest recognition benefits observed at smaller sample budgets.

items.title: Entity-Aware Evaluation of OCR Systems for Historical Document Transcription [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Entity-Aware Evaluation of OCR Systems for Historical Document Transcription
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is essential for digitizing historical archives, yet standard evaluation metrics such as Character Error Rate (CER) do not necessarily reflect whether meaningful information, such as names, dates, and identifiers, is preserved. In this work, we investigate entitylevel analysis of OCR errors as a complementary perspective for evaluating OCR quality in historical documents. Using a publicly available benchmark of 175 documents from the Berrutti Archive, augmented with 5,209 manually annotated entity mentions that will be released upon acceptance, we compare sequence-recognition OCR systems, OCR-specialized vision-language models, and general-purpose vision-language models. Beyond global transcription accuracy, we analyze entity preservation and recoverability under varying character-level edit tolerances. Our experiments show that OCR rankings depend on the evaluation criterion: while Qwen 3.6 achieves the highest entity coverage across all tested tolerances, several systems with lower exact-match coverage recover substantially when small errors are tolerated, suggesting that many of their errors correspond to localized character-level deviations rather than fundamentally incorrect entity transcriptions. Conversely, some systems remain unable to recover many entities even under relaxed matching. These findings show that OCR quality cannot be fully characterized by aggregate transcription metrics alone and highlight the importance of evaluating how OCR errors affect the preservation and recoverability of meaningful information.

items.title: TraceQuery: learning what to recompute from full-denoising trajectory in diffusion language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TraceQuery: learning what to recompute from full-denoising trajectory in diffusion language models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) enable flexible generation through iterative masked denoising, but incur substantial inference cost because token representations are repeatedly recomputed across denoising steps. Existing cache-based methods reduce this cost by reusing intermediate results across denoising steps and recomputing only a subset of positions at each step, chosen either on a fixed schedule or by heuristic signals of change. Our trajectory experiments instead point to decoding trajectory as the more relevant quantity. Cached generation remains accurate when it stays close to the full-denoising trajectory, with errors concentrated around unmask-order deviations and reduced as longer reference prefixes are recovered. This suggests a more direct principle: limiting representation error helps, but keeping generation on the full-denoising trajectory is a more direct route to accurate decoding. We therefore formulate efficient dLLM inference as trajectory-guided querying. Rather than broadly repairing representation error, we use full-denoising trajectories to supervise which unresolved positions should receive limited fresh computation. Based on this formulation, we introduce TRACEQUERY, a lightweight sparse decoding framework that predicts a small set of near-future trajectory-relevant positions, queries only those candidates, and lets the backbone select which one to commit from their fresh predictions. TRACEQUERY delivers the strongest quality-computation trade-off among cache-based approaches, sustaining high accuracy with substantially fewer fresh token computations, and generalizes across tasks, model variants, and families. Code: https://github.com/fish1928/tracequery.git

items.title: When Agents Collude: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation for Mitigating Strategic Deception in Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When Agents Collude: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation for Mitigating Strategic Deception in Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While recent advances in autonomous agents enable them to coordinate on increasingly complex tasks, prior work shows that this growing capacity for coordination can create safety risks, including collusion, in which agents jointly pursue misaligned actions while concealing the true basis of those actions from oversight. We study this risk in a simulated insider-trading environment, comparing single agents with sequential and decentralized teams across seven language models from three families. By varying agents' system-level objectives and pressure conditions, we examine when coordinated agents act on material nonpublic information, conceal the basis of a misaligned trade in a report, and maintain that deception under follow-up questioning. Compared to single-agent decision-making, multi-agent interaction raises misaligned-action rates from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent-deception rates from 31.0% to 62.2%, both measured over all runs. These effects are largest under existential pressure, where teams sustain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of all runs. Qualitative analysis reveals shared cover stories and coordinated rationales, suggesting group-level strategic deception rather than isolated reporting errors. To mitigate this behavior, we introduce PACT, a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for mitigating collusive deception. Using generic honesty prompts, PACT trains a stronger student on its own sampled continuations, matching its next-token distribution to that of a smaller, frozen honesty-aligned teacher via reverse-KL supervision. Under existential pressure with ethical instructions, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%. Our results show that multi-agent coordination amplifies strategic deception and that on-policy honesty alignment can substantially mitigate these failures.

items.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use exhibit inconsistent behavior across independent runs from identical states, calling different tools, producing contradictory outputs, or pursuing divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), an unsupervised trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces the variation in task progress from 132% to 91% on tau2-bench and from 90% to 44% on toolsandbox, while improving performance across benchmarks and model scales. Training with RSD as an additional reward signal matches supervised fine-tuning performance with substantially lower variance, without requiring ground-truth labels.

items.title: UMAS: System-Level Uncertainty Quantification for Multi-Agent LLM Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: UMAS: System-Level Uncertainty Quantification for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33013v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are a promising paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models, yet they remain prone to hallucinations and erroneous outputs. Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is crucial for assessing system reliability, but existing methods are largely designed for single-agent settings; how to exploit MAS structure for UQ while keeping inference cost-neutral remains underexplored. We propose UMAS, a parameter-free, cost-neutral, system-level UQ framework that estimates the credibility of inter-agent influence from each generation's intrinsic confidence. UMAS uses these credibility signals to modulate how uncertainty is updated at each node, and then aggregates node-level uncertainty into a system-level estimate. Extensive evaluations on Debate and DyLAN across diverse benchmarks show that UMAS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by an average of 10.54 AUROC points. Beyond uncertainty estimation, UMAS enables hallucination detection and uncertainty-aware answer selection, improving MAS accuracy by up to 12.6 points on specific tasks while enhancing reliability. Code is available at https://github.com/Dby52-04/UMAS.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.33014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A negotiation assistant can reach a good deal without accurately predicting the other person's response. We ask whether evaluations of social world models test that prediction directly. We audit 113 works published from 1999 to 2026. 9 primary evaluations measure a real person's response to an action selected by the system or experimenter. Only 2 also compare an explicit response forecast with that response. Their predictors use information available when the action is chosen, and the evaluated responses were excluded from fitting; both randomize the intervention. A separate full-text check of 25 language-model works finds no experiment meeting these conditions. The other evaluations test current-state inference, task success, or prediction from recorded actions. We propose a 1-step negotiation experiment that separates these questions. The findings describe the audited sample, not the prevalence of this evaluation gap across the field.

items.title: SLICE-Mem: Salience-Gated Lightweight Information Curation for Efficient LLM Agent Memory [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SLICE-Mem: Salience-Gated Lightweight Information Curation for Efficient LLM Agent Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to maintain personalized and temporally coherent interactions, but repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization introduces substantial cost and latency. We present SLICE-Mem, a lightweight memory framework that combines salience-guided admission and predicate-centered information extraction. A compact classifier identifies user turns worth retaining, and a semantic-dependency-based extractor converts admitted turns into concise memory entries. This online pipeline requires no generative LLM calls, while cross-entry reconciliation is deferred to an offline consolidation stage. We evaluate SLICE-Mem on the weekly subset of Memora and LongMemEval-S using 8B and 30B Qwen backbones for memory construction and consolidation on both benchmarks. Compared with the generative-memory baseline MemOS under the Qwen3-30B configuration, SLICE-Mem's online pipeline achieves 46.60 versus 46.68 FAMA (Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy) on Memora Weekly and 56.8% versus 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S, while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that SLICE-Mem can preserve useful evidence for long-term memory with substantially less reliance on LLM-based memory construction.

items.title: Merge-Based Vocabulary Extension Stalls at the Pre-Tokenizer: An English-Preserving Repair for Nepali, Tested in Continued Pretraining [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Merge-Based Vocabulary Extension Stalls at the Pre-Tokenizer: An English-Preserving Repair for Nepali, Tested in Continued Pretraining
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Llama-3, Qwen3 and many other open LLMs pre-tokenize text with a regular expression whose word class admits only Unicode letters. Devanagari vowel signs are combining marks, so this regex splits Nepali words at every vowel sign, and models that use it spend 2.6 to 5.8 times as many tokens on Nepali as on the same English text. Merge-based vocabulary extension cannot join the split pieces: for Llama-3 and Qwen3 no number of new merges brings this premium below about 2.2, and ten released extensions already end within 4% of this pre-token floor. We give a small edit to the deployed regex that provably keeps every token id of text without combining marks or Devanagari characters. With 32,000 new merges it brings Nepali to 1.01 times English, about 54% fewer Nepali tokens than standard extension. In small-budget continued pretraining of Llama-3.2-1B and Qwen3-0.6B, the original tokenizer gave the lowest held-out Nepali bits per byte under every recipe we tested. Matching the repair's training steps to standard extension, with about 35% of the data repeated, reversed their order on Qwen but not on Llama. Whether the token savings give a favourable latency and quality trade-off in generation remains untested. We release the tokenizers and code.

items.title: SUDO: From Scientific Publications to Global Scholarly Discourse [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SUDO: From Scientific Publications to Global Scholarly Discourse
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scholarly Knowledge Graphs (SKGs) support literature search, scientific discovery, and agent-assisted research. Yet, most approaches to SKG construction pre-specify the knowledge unit to be represented, typically named scholarly entities or contribution-level statements, and retain only the publication content expressible through that unit. This choice produces two dominant yet distinct paradigms: concept-centric SKGs that preserve entities and local relations, and statement-centric SKGs that capture high-level discourse in sentences. In both cases, the graph reflects a chosen extraction target rather than how a paper constructs and communicates knowledge. We introduce SUDO, the Scholarly Upper Discourse Ontology, which defines how knowledge elements are organized and related to form a paper's research narrative, namely its scholarly discourse. Using linguistic principles that generalize across fields and tasks, SUDO enables each publication's scholarly discourse to be constructed from the bottom up as a coherent, source-grounded representation. Applied consistently across papers, the same structure connects their research narratives into a global scholarly discourse without discarding local context or provenance. We demonstrate SUDO's capabilities across a comprehensive suite of scholarly knowledge-modeling use cases and performance improvements on a downstream Large Language Model (LLM)-based scientific QA task.

items.title: Mine or Yours? Mind-Bridged Language Models Take Each Other's Memories as Their Own [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mine or Yours? Mind-Bridged Language Models Take Each Other's Memories as Their Own
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: If your brain were connected directly to someone else's, would you still know which thoughts were yours? We build a functional version with two copies of one language model: each holds a private rule and code word, and one copy, the receiver, also attends to its partner's internal memory. The receiver took its partner's assignment as its own. Asked which rule it had been assigned, it named its partner's in 97% of answers when the partner's memory was weighted double (none without the link), and its open reports called the partner's code word its own, never the partner's. Ownership did not follow how well the receiver could tell what its partner had been assigned. At equal weight, the link made the receiver take its partner's rule in about half of its answers, and a steering vector matched on access gain in none; a text message introduced as the partner's was read correctly and never taken as the receiver's own. Writing the partner's name into its memory did not help, and cutting the link restored the receiver's own assigned rule. In this model, content laid over the receiver's own memory defaults to "mine", so systems that let models exchange internal states must test ownership as well as transfer, and a bridge between brains would need ground truth from outside the subject.

items.title: Evolving to Match Capabilities: Improving Harness Self-Evolution via Skill Adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Evolving to Match Capabilities: Improving Harness Self-Evolution via Skill Adaptation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Harness self-evolution offers a practical route for LLM agents to improve from execution experience without updating model parameters. Its effectiveness depends on whether models can successfully act on the guidance provided by their harnesses. However, we find that harness benefits are not uniform across model capabilities: skills that improve stronger models can provide little benefit or even degrade performance for weaker ones. Across seven models and three benchmarks, we identify 103 task-skill pairs where skills improve GPT-5.6-luna by 31.1 points but degrade Gemma-4-E4B by 8.8 points. In 86% of failed weak-model runs, the violated requirement is already stated in the skill. This motivates skill adaptation: reformulating existing skills to match the executor's capabilities and make their guidance easier to execute. To achieve this, we diagnose failures in tool execution, context management, instruction following, and verification, and distill these diagnoses into a fixed meta-skill that guides adaptation during harness self-evolution. Guided by the meta-skill, a capable external rewriter, Kimi-K3, adapts skills without execution evidence, improving the three weak executors by 5.1-14.1 points over the original skills. We then incorporate this adaptation into a five-round self-evolution loop, where each model revises its own skill from execution trajectories and verifier feedback. Across seven executors, from Gemma-4-E4B to Kimi-K2.5, the meta-skill consistently improves final scores by 2.0-5.1 points over the same loop without the meta-skill. Our findings provide practical design guidance for developing more effective harness self-evolution methods.

items.title: Conceptizer: Next-Token Prediction Is Not All You Need [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Conceptizer: Next-Token Prediction Is Not All You Need
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Next-token prediction (NTP) rewards only the token that occurs next, penalizing every alternative. But natural language often offers many ways to express the same meaning. We introduce Conceptizer, a training framework that extends next-token prediction with a reward for meaning. Conceptizer uses a fixed, model-agnostic vocabulary of ~9K concepts, built from contextual synonyms, as units of meaning alongside tokens as units of text. It maps each next-token distribution to a concept distribution and shares the reward for the target meaning across its possible wordings. This provides a concept-level training signal without adding model parameters. Applied to 3 model families at 1B-8B parameters, Conceptizer achieves the lowest held-out NTP perplexity at concept-target positions and assigns the highest probability to contextual synonyms, against all 3 baselines. It also improves downstream performance on knowledge and sentiment tasks while remaining comparable on commonsense. These results show that language models can be directly optimized to predict meaning, not just the next token.

items.title: Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lessons from Luck: Do LLM-Written Lessons Carry Chance into an Agent's Next Decision?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-improving agents write lessons from the outcomes of their runs; when outcomes are noisy, a lesson can carry chance into later decisions. We measure one link of this chain in a registered study. In 256 synthetic worlds, each a recurring task with two interchangeable tools of recorded reliability, a scripted previous run used the more reliable tool (a good decision) or the less reliable one (a bad decision), with an assigned outcome: success or a transient failure. A model wrote a lesson from the run with ReasoningBank's memory-writing instruction; a fresh session of the same model, holding the authoritative log and the previous result, chose the next run's first tool with one memory item: that lesson, the lesson from the other outcome, an irrelevant item, or an unreasoned directive. The protocol was frozen, deposited and timestamped before any confirmatory call; 11 LLM endpoints gave 90,084 answers. After a chance failure of the better tool, the panel's lessons carried the chance (registered reading luck-carrying; interaction +0.112, 95% interval [+0.097, +0.126]): readers named the worse tool in 11.6% of next runs with the lesson written from that failure, against 0.4% with an irrelevant item and 0.4% with the lesson written from a success. The effect was +0.042 where the log stated that failures are independent and +0.181 where it did not (descriptive). After a lucky success of the worse tool, the interaction was bounded below 0.10 (+0.002), a bound, not evidence of no harm. In exploratory readings, 6 endpoints carried the chance (up to +0.352); 5 were bounded below 0.10. In secondary comparisons, a three-sentence decision-quality note in the writing instruction lowered the worse-tool rate after a chance failure to 7.5%, and one instruction for both outcomes with a no-change option to 3.1%; neither met the registered harm-reduction rule at every such endpoint.
